description: A deep-sea typing-defense game in one standalone file. Open it in any browser and start typing.

title: Getting Up Here
description: A silly clone of Getting Over It by Bennett Foddy.

title: Downhill Dreamer — a hill-surfing bird game
description: Hold to dive, release to soar! Surf procedurally generated hills as a little round bird, chain perfect slides, break the sound barrier and outrun the night in this free browser game.

title: Timberbound — a first-person voxel incremental about impossible trees
description: Timberbound is a first-person voxel incremental game about felling increasingly impossible trees, hauling strange lumber to a shopkeeper called Mosswick, and becoming gloriously overpowered. Eight forests, eleven axes, a 30-node skill constellation, spreading wildfire and a drone fleet that hauls millions of logs for you.

title: Mastermind — 3D Code-Breaking Game with Move Analysis
description: Break the hidden code in a 3D Mastermind board with a generative soundtrack. Play 4 or 5 slots, 6 or 8 colours, then see exactly how many of the possible codes each of your guesses ruled out.

title: Pulseforge — a rhythm game that composes its own songs
description: A four-lane rhythm game with no audio files. Type any word as a seed and Pulseforge composes a full track — drums, bass, pads and a melody that is the note chart itself. Play it on keyboard or touch, then share the seed.

title: Lumenwright — a laser puzzle about bending light into colour
description: Rotate mirrors, prisms, beam splitters and dichroic mirrors until every detector receives exactly the colour it asks for. Endless generated levels that keep changing shape, a daily puzzle, and an exact par for every board. No downloads, no assets, plays on keyboard or touch.

title: Glyphgate — a deduction game about laws you have to discover
description: The gate admits some rows of glyphs and turns others away, and it will not say why. Run experiments, narrow it down, and state the law. Thirteen gates each teach a new kind of rule, answers are judged by meaning rather than wording, and every wrong answer hands back the shortest row that refutes it.

title: Selfsame — a puzzle game about cooperating with your past selves
description: Every room gives you one short hour. Spend it and the you who spent it stays behind as an echo, repeating every step forever — so you plan the next hour around it. Twenty-two hand-built rooms of plates, shutters, crates and orbs, every one shipped with a verified solution and a par proved minimal by exhaustive search.

title: Escapement — a pinball machine that builds a clock
description: Real pinball physics in a single file: flippers you can cradle a ball on, ramps you have to hit hard enough to make, slingshots, a spinner, drop targets and a centre scoop. Every mission you finish installs another part of a clock, and the part is then physically on the playfield — a kickback, a turning escape wheel, a second habitrail, chime bars, an upper flipper. Build all five and the clock can strike twelve. No downloads, keyboard or touch.

title: Nine Holes — procedural minigolf you can ace
description: A round of nine procedurally generated minigolf holes. Every one is checked before you see it: a hole-in-one is always possible, but never by simply pointing at the cup — the ace window is a couple of degrees wide and you have to find it. Slopes push the ball, bumpers throw it back, sand kills it, water costs a stroke, and the cup spits the ball out if it arrives too fast. Par is measured by playing each hole rather than guessed, and the nine are ordered gentlest first. Drag to putt or aim with the arrow keys. Share a round by its seed.

title: Everywhere — write one rule that solves every maze
description: A programming puzzle where you never solve a level. You write one short rulebook for a robot — plain if-then lines, read top to bottom and then repeated — and the game tests it against hundreds of mazes you have never seen, then shows you the one that beats it, with your robot's path drawn on it. Eight stages take you from a straight corridor to the wall-following rule that solves every maze, then start taking the robot's senses away and make you rebuild it blind. Below them is The Deep, an endless run of handicaps drawn from an exhaustive table of which vocabularies can solve a maze at all — so every round is known to be beatable, and tells you in how many lines.

title: Scatter — Pac-Man with the ghost AI made visible
description: The 1980 maze chase, rebuilt with the ghost logic intact. The maze is the original one — 240 pellets and four energizers — and the ghosts are not four copies of "walk toward Pac-Man": Blinky targets your tile, Pinky aims four ahead to cut you off (with the original's overflow bug when you face up), Inky doubles a vector through Blinky, and Clyde loses his nerve inside eight tiles. Scatter and chase waves, the dot counters that release each ghost, cornering, tunnel slowdown and Blinky's endgame speed-up are all in. A strip under the board counts down to the next scatter — the window the arcade never showed you — and flipping on the target overlay makes every ghost draw a line to the tile it has chosen, so you can watch the most-studied AI in games decide. A practice mode slows the ghosts if you want to learn the maze first.

title: Hummingbird — a game you play by humming
description: A singing game. Hum, sing or whistle and a little bird follows your voice along a flower vine — hold the line and the flowers bloom behind you. It listens to your range first, then writes songs that fit your voice: seven meadows that add leaps, take away the guide note singing along with you, narrow the vine, and finally drop the band out altogether so you have to hold the tune alone and come back in tune when they return. Every melody is grown and then judged before you hear it, so it stays singable. No microphone? Fly her with the mouse.

title: Strata — a falling-sand world you have to discover
description: A falling-sand sandbox with no palette. You start with sand, water, stone, fire and a seed; the other twenty-nine materials have to be found. Quench lava to get obsidian, let steam climb until it snows, bury a plant deep under stone and come back to find oil, then coal, then diamond. The ground is opaque until you cut into it, so the salt seams, the ore and the magma at the bottom are yours to dig out. Nothing is discovered for you. Slow the world to an eighth speed to watch a reaction happen, or switch on high-contrast colours to tell the greys apart. Your notebook is kept between worlds.

title: Alibi — a game for two people and one phone
description: You and a friend swear you were together last night. The phone is the detective: it asks you both the same question, you answer in secret and pass it over, and then it shows you whether your two stories match. Every answer costs something — an account nobody can confirm costs more, one with a witness in it costs less, and anything the detective is hot on costs more each time you lean on it, so the safe answer stops being safe. Agree your story out loud before it starts, because you don't get to talk again. Sixteen places, ten crimes, three scenes a night, and a written statement at the end with every crack in it marked.

title: Procession — a deck-builder that never shuffles
description: Nine fights, one new card after each, and a deck that is never shuffled. At the end of every turn the cards you played drop to the bottom in the order you played them, and the cards you held follow behind — so the hand you draw three turns from now is one you dealt yourself. Nothing is hidden: you can see the next five cards and the enemy states its exact next move, so anything that kills you was something you could see coming. Cards you play together come back together, which makes spacing your plays as much of the game as choosing them. Four ways to build — force, guard, venom and tempo — each with one card that pays off enormously if you built for it and does almost nothing if you didn't. Seeded, so a run can be handed to someone else.

title: Jigsaw
description: Drop in a photo and it becomes a real interlocking jigsaw — pieces that snap together and from then on move as one lump, the way a jigsaw actually behaves. 12 to 540 pieces, an optional rotation mode, four procedural pictures if you have no photo to hand, and it remembers where you got to. Nothing ever leaves your browser.

title: Menagerie
description: Sculpt a world and watch animals evolve to cross it. Nobody designs them: eighty are thrown together at random — a back, some legs, a rhythm — and whichever get furthest have the children. The population breeds as separate species, one per body plan, so a two-limbed hopper and an eight-limbed crawler can develop side by side instead of the first winner swallowing the run. Every world sets a distance to beat: raise hills, dig flooded trenches, pull down a roof they must crawl under, or ice the floor, and each one breeds a different animal. Keep the ones you like on the shelf and release them somewhere they were never bred for.

title: Fresh Oil — bowling where the lane is the opponent
description: Ten frames of tenpin with the physics actually simulated, not faked: the ball is a rigid body with a real inertia tensor, so it hooks because friction acts on a spinning sphere, and the drilling layout decides how much fresh cover it puts down each revolution. Forty feet of oil lie between you and the pocket, and every ball thrown on the lane — yours and the three other bowlers on the pair — takes a little of it away. The line that struck in the first frame comes in high by the sixth. Read where your ball arrived, move two boards with your feet and one with your eyes, and keep chasing the lane until the tenth.

title: Shopfloor — a factory that only gets one screen
description: A factory-building puzzle on a floor that never grows. Machines face the way you point them and only take what their recipe asks for, so a wrong turn parks an ingot at a press door and stops the line behind it. Ore comes in at a fixed rate however many ports you open, belts cost budget just like machines do, and six orders keep asking for something the layout you just built cannot make — so you spend the shift tearing up your own factory.

title: Liquid War — an army that follows your cursor
description: Your army is a few thousand fighters and you command none of them: you move one cursor, and every fighter of your colour floods through the maze along the shortest path to it. When two colours meet nobody dies — the loser changes sides, so the map is a tug of war over one fixed population and every fight you win makes you bigger. Feed a corridor one fighter at a time and you hand it over; pull back until the queue bunches up and arrive all at once, and you take it. Seeded battlefields in six shapes, up to four armies, five opposing temperaments and a twelve-battle ladder that bends one rule at a time.

title: Blobby Volley
description: The beach-volleyball classic, rebuilt on the original game's physics constants: the ball always leaves a blob at exactly the same speed, so you aim by where on your body you meet it, never by hitting harder. Serve-side scoring to 15, three touches a side, and a net post that eats the ball. Play a friend on one keyboard, a computer opponent that reads the ball's landing point, or either of those on a phone.

title: Icy Tower
description: The tower climb built on one rule from the original: horizontal speed is the only thing that lifts you. A standing jump clears two floors, a full sprint thirteen — so you run the length of a floor, or bounce off a wall and flick your direction back on impact to keep every bit of momentum. Multi-floor landings chain into combos worth their length squared, the floors start sinking at floor 5 and pull harder every thirty seconds, and the seed in the URL makes any tower repeatable.

title: Moor Chicken
description: The moor chicken hunt of 1999, rebuilt on the numbers that made it work: ninety seconds, ten shells to a magazine, and a reload that costs you time you cannot spare. The moor is three screens wide and you swing the barrel across it, so the skill is not marksmanship but choosing targets — a speck near the horizon pays 20, the fat one under your nose pays 5, the windmill's four blades and the scarecrow's hat pay 25 apiece, and the signpost costs you 25. Seeded moors, mouse or thumbs.

title: Pingu Throw
description: The 2004 yeti classic, rebuilt on its two clicks: one sends the penguin diving off the ice wall, the other swings the club the instant you press it — no wind-up, exactly as in the original, so the whole game is how level the penguin is with the club head when you tap. Dead level is 52 metres per second at 38 degrees and six bounces; a hand too high lobs it steeply, a hand too low skids it flat, and either way it still flies. No air control, no wind, no RNG: the same tap gives the same number every time — which is why your best can fly beside you as a ghost, and a challenge link hands a friend your exact throw to race.

title: Peg Fever
description: The 2007 peg-dropping classic, rebuilt on the numbers that make it tick: 25 orange pegs to clear, 10 balls to do it with, blue pegs worth 10 and orange worth 100 — and each peg a single drop touches is worth more than the last, so the tenth peg of a rally pays ten times the first. The fever meter lifts the whole board to x2, x3, x5 and x10 as the oranges fall, the free-ball bucket sweeps the base, long shots pay 25,000, and the last orange peg opens the five bonus slots. Three powers, seeded boards, drag to aim with a thumb.

title: Worms
description: Worms Armageddon rebuilt on the numbers that make it work: terrain is a pixel mask, so a crater is the exact shape the explosion had; a worm is a 9x16 coffin that climbs 8px without jumping; wind is a constant acceleration that bends a bazooka a hundred pixels across a long shot and does nothing at all to a grenade. Sixteen weapons and utilities including a ninja rope you can wrap round corners, girders that survive blasts, a jetpack and an air strike. 2 to 4 teams, each human or CPU, hot-seat on one device; the CPU solves its shot by simulating arcs against the real terrain. Seeded maps, sudden death, and thumb controls that keep both pads under your hands.

title: Kurve
description: Achtung, die Kurve! (Zatacka, 1995) rebuilt on measurements taken off the original DOS binary under DOSBox: a 559x480 field, 70 pixels a second, a smallest turning circle 57 pixels across, a 3-pixel trail, and a hole punched in that trail every 195 pixels that is 8 pixels long — the hole is the whole game, because without it the field locks solid. Up to six players on one keyboard with the original key pairs down to the mouse-button player, a lobby you join by pressing your own key, bots to fill the field, two thumbs each for two players on a phone, and a seed in the URL so a match replays exactly.

title: Tilt Maze
description: The Brio wooden labyrinth in a browser tab, and the rare page here that is better on a phone than on a desktop: you tilt the actual phone. The ball is a solid steel sphere rolling without slipping, so it accelerates at (5/7)g·sin θ rather than g·sin θ — two sevenths of gravity goes into spin, and that factor is the difference between a ball and a cursor. Rolling resistance, a restitution measured for steel on wood, and a 60 Hz sim split into substeps short enough that a fast ball can never cross a 6 mm wall without hitting it. On iOS the motion permission is asked from the Start button, beta and gamma are rotated by the screen angle so landscape does not tip the board sideways, and a Re-zero button means you never have to hold the phone flat. No sensor: the mouse or the arrow keys tilt the same board, to the same limits. Five boards, one clock, and every board proved before you see it — a flood fill on the ball's centre finds a route with 3 mm of clearance either side, and any hole that would sever the last one is never placed. Seed in the URL.

title: Five Rungs
description: Five daily puzzles on one page, and deliberately five different kinds rather than one kind five times over: a region-logic board, an arithmetic grid, a polyomino packing, a word ladder and a country hunt that answers in kilometres and compass points. The date is the only seed, so there is no server and everybody gets the same five — at midnight UTC, written on the page, because local midnight would mean two people on the same calendar day comparing different puzzles. Because the date is the seed an archive costs nothing, so every past day is still playable, which the commercial versions of this genre cannot do. Nothing here is hand-written per day and nothing is authored: each puzzle is generated and then handed to a solver before it is shown. Lanterns and Ledger must come out by deduction with no guessing; Tessera and Lanterns are counted exhaustively for a single answer; Rungs is a breadth-first count of shortest chains, so exactly one ladder of that length exists. Over 220 consecutive days every puzzle generated and every one was unique. Emoji result grids per puzzle and one combined block, showing the run and never the answer, and a streak that survives a private window by falling back to memory.

title: Rack
description: A crossword tile game on the classic 15×15 board: seven letters, premium squares, blanks, the 50-point bonus for using all seven. Play a computer opponent or pass one device between up to four people, each rack hidden behind a cover until its owner taps. The referee is a 270,000-word list; the easy and medium computers only play everyday words, so what they put down is something you could have found yourself rather than USQUE, and hard knows the whole list and keeps a balanced rack. After each of your moves the log shows the best play you had, and the end of the game says what share of the available points you took. A seed in the URL deals the same tiles again.

title: Bubble Break — a bubble wrap incremental
description: An incremental about popping bubble wrap on your coffee break. Press bubbles one at a time until your thumb is strong enough to swipe, hold down on the thick ones, grab the gold before the machine does its rounds, chase sugar rushes and pop zippers that open whole rows. Quit your job for calluses, finish orders to take more with you, and work your way from the office desk through a warehouse and a factory to a city on moving day, where one sheet holds tens of millions of bubbles and a loop of cordon tape pops a million at once. Then wrap the world and pop it, and everything after it.

title: Firefly Jar
description: A cozy incremental made of summer nights. Sweep the jar, which follows your mouse or finger, through the fireflies as fast as you like. Carry a full jar to the lantern before dawn takes it, and spend the light on a skill tree that is a real tree of hanging lanterns. Turning the season is the prestige: the crown goes dark, the roots keep tree rings, and every season brings something new to do instead of a bigger number. Will-o'-wisp trails lay paths home across the autumn moor, icicles split the light into coloured beams and an aurora dips into the winter meadow, spring buds keep light and pay it back with interest, and Midsummer grows the meadow into a forest until the fireflies rise into the Milky Way. Along the way a field journal fills with the real species you learn to tell by their light: glow-worms in the grass, the steady blue ghost, the synchronous fireflies of the Smoky Mountains that flash in bursts all together, and the femme fatale that fakes other species' signals to eat them. The meadow, the trees and the soundtrack are all made in code, with a tune of its own for each season: electric piano and guitar in summer, a harp waltz in autumn, a music box in winter and a flute in spring. About two hours from the first jar to the credits; progress is saved in the browser.
